papers.title: Machine Learning Methods for Automatic Sleep Stage Classification: Current Status and Future Challenges.
papers.abstract: The intricacies of sleep architecture hold significant implications for understanding human health, making automated sleep staging a critical frontier in sleep research. While existing literature predominantly delves into deep learning methods for sleep staging, the current landscape of lightweight, home-use sleep monitoring devices necessitates a closer examination of traditional machine learning algorithms for sleep pattern recognition and analysis. In response to this need, in this paper we provide a comprehensive review of machine learning methods for automatic sleep staging. By synthesizing state-of-the-art approaches, we traverse the entire process, from data collection devices to feature extraction and selection, culminating in diverse sleep stage classification methods. These methods encompass single-modality, dual-modality, and multi-modality approaches, reflecting the evolving complexity of sleep stage classification methodologies. Moreover, we delve into the challenges, identify emerging trends, and outline future directions in the field of sleep staging. By offering these insights, we aim to equip researchers, clinicians, and technologists with a roadmap for advancing automated sleep staging methodologies within the realm of machine learning.

ai.reason: Comprehensive review of lightweight traditional ML sleep staging covering feature extraction, modalities, and home-use devices—directly aligned with core interests.
ai.summary: Reviews machine learning methods for automatic sleep stage classification, covering the full pipeline from data collection devices through feature extraction and selection to single-, dual-, and multi-modality classifiers, and outlines challenges and future directions with emphasis on lightweight home-use monitoring.

papers.title: GamSleepNet: A Lightweight Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Based on Gabor Feature Extraction and Mamba Sequence Modeling for Single-Channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for the precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders and for long-term home sleep monitoring. Due to its convenience of use, single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) has become a research focus in home sleep monitoring. However, existing algorithms still face several practical bottlenecks. For example, models with a large number of parameters are prone to overfitting on small labeled datasets; the hardware heterogeneity of customized portable sensors makes datasets not directly shareable; large-scale labeled samples are hard to obtain in real scenarios; there is low recognition accuracy for difficult-to-distinguish sleep stages such as N1 and REM; and there is a lack of suitable research methods for evaluating the required scale of training data for lightweight deployment scenarios. In this paper we propose GamSleepNet, a low-parameter-count automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework combines a feature extraction module (FEB), which integrates improved Gabor kernels with a learnable filter branch, with a standard Mamba selective state-space model (SSM) used for temporal modeling. A teacher-student feature alignment loss (FAL) and a two-stage training strategy are introduced to enhance the discriminative ability for difficult sleep stages. In addition, following the established paradigm of varying the training dataset's size and observing the performance curve, we make four adaptations tailored to sleep staging, thereby determining the appropriate training data volume for GamSleepNet and providing a methodological reference for determining the training data scale required for deploying other models. Under the limited-labeled-subject setting of the Sleep-EDF dataset, the model has 30.86 k parameters and achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86% and a macro F1 score of 82.62%-the highest values among the compared models-and improves the recognition of difficult REM and N1 samples. The model still maintains stable staging performance under low signal-to-noise ratio and label-scarce scenarios.

papers.title: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting.
papers.abstract: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

ai.summary: Developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable EEG in which a five-stage sleep classifier (M0) fed cross-fitted stage-probability histories to a second layer (M1) forecasting transitions from wake/N1 to N2/N3/REM within 60-120 s. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1, and M1 reached AUROC 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s respectively, with cross-device limitations identified on Muse S Gen2 recordings.

papers.title: Identification of Insomnia Disorder Using Machine Learning and Wearable Technology.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a prevalent sleep disorder. Wearable electroencephalography (EEG) combined with machine learning (ML) offers a promising, low-burden approach for home-based sleep monitoring and objective assessment of insomnia. The study included 112 patients with insomnia disorder (ID) and 98 healthy controls (HC), who underwent overnight forehead EEG recording. For each subject, macro-sleep metrics, as well as EEG-derived features including aperiodic and periodic features, were extracted. To classify ID and HC, we constructed predictive models based on three feature categories and their combinations. Specifically, we trained five ML models, namely Elastic Net, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost and CatBoost. All models performed significantly better than chance. Performance was highest for feature sets including periodic features, with the CatBoost periodic and macro + periodic models achieving the highest AUC (0.765). SHAP analysis of the full-feature CatBoost model showed that delta-band power and sleep timing ranked at the top, whereas aperiodic features contributed less but remained informative. This study explored the value of objective metrics derived from wearable sleep devices in insomnia assessment and the role of aperiodic and periodic sleep features. These findings support the hyperarousal model of insomnia and the feasibility of wearable sleep monitoring as a low-burden adjunct for insomnia assessment.

ai.summary: Used overnight forehead wearable EEG with five machine learning models to classify 112 insomnia disorder patients versus 98 healthy controls; CatBoost models including periodic features reached the highest AUC (0.765), and SHAP ranked delta-band power and sleep timing as top contributors.

papers.title: MG-STNet: A Compact Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Network for Adaptive Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging from polysomnography (PSG) is a core component of objective sleep analysis and plays a crucial role in enabling reliable clinical assessment and downstream physiological interpretation, yet the non-stationary nature of physiological signals poses significant challenges for compact models with fixed temporal receptive fields that cannot adapt to time-varying sleep rhythms. To address this challenge, we propose MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for adaptive sleep staging. The model first utilizes a Multi-Granularity Feature Learning Module (MFLM) to extract multi-resolution representations via parallel downsampling branches, thereby reducing sequence length and computational redundancy. Building on this compact representation, the Global-Local Feature Recalibration (GLFR) module recalibrates multi-channel PSG features by jointly leveraging global statistics and local temporal interactions, while the Adaptive Spatiotemporal Convolution (ASTC) module dynamically routes among complementary temporal branches to capture evolving sleep rhythms. Furthermore, a Temporal Attention Encoding Module (TAEM) is integrated to model long-range dependencies within each epoch. We evaluate MG-STNet on Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 using subject-independent k-fold cross-validation. The four-channel model achieves accuracies of 87.3% and 84.5% with 46.6K parameters and 17.2M FLOPs, while its single-channel counterpart achieves 86.6% and 83.2% with 48.6K parameters and 9.8M FLOPs. Experimental results indicate that MG-STNet achieves competitive accuracy with a substantially smaller parameter footprint than mainstream deep sleep-staging models, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for automatic sleep staging under computational constraints.

ai.reason: Compact, adaptive spatiotemporal PSG sleep staging aligns strongly with lightweight, generalizable sleep classification interests.
ai.summary: Proposed MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for sleep staging using parallel downsampling branches, global-local feature recalibration, adaptive spatiotemporal convolution, and temporal attention encoding. On Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 it achieved 87.3% and 84.5% accuracy (four-channel, 46.6K parameters) and 86.6% and 83.2% (single-channel), offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: Operational Definitions of Transition Onset Shape EEG Biomarker Timing in Drowsiness: A Single-Channel Method Comparison.
papers.abstract: Early-warning claims for electroencephalography (EEG)-based drowsiness detection rest on lead times, yet a lead time depends on how onset is operationally defined and is rarely tested against a null. We developed a benchmarking framework and applied it to seven onset estimators and 32 features from single-channel frontal EEG (17 participants, observer-verified drowsiness reports), with external replication in the DROZY dataset (13 sessions with an eligible vigilance-lapse anchor, of 20 retained). Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and changed detection coverage from 45% to 100% (Kendall's W = 0.53; external W = 0.71; absolute-agreement intraclass correlation 0.05). In simulation, two-standard-deviation baseline rules flagged onsets in 77-88% of no-change trajectories; null-calibrated thresholds (about 4.6 standard deviations) restored a nominal 5% rate. No estimator showed a statistically detectable excess of onsets in the final 150 s before the anchor relative to spectrum-preserving surrogates, a consensus detector fired before pseudo-anchors as often as before the true anchor, and adding EEG to elapsed session time gave no detectable improvement (area-under-the-curve difference 0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.11 to 0.13). Higuchi fractal dimension and line length correlated weakly with measured electrooculography (|r| ≤ 0.15). We propose interpretability criteria, evidence levels and a reporting checklist for early-onset claims.

ai.topic: Benchmarking onset definitions for EEG drowsiness detection
ai.reason: Rigorous single-channel vigilance-onset benchmarking with null controls is highly relevant to sleep/vigilance state detection methodology.
ai.summary: Built a benchmarking framework to test how operational definitions of transition onset affect EEG drowsiness lead-time claims, applying seven onset estimators and 32 single-channel frontal EEG features across 17 participants with replication in DROZY. Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and detection coverage ranged from 45% to 100%, while no estimator showed excess pre-anchor onsets versus surrogate data, prompting proposed interpretability criteria, evidence levels, and a reporting checklist.

papers.title: Pre-anaesthetic anxiety phenotype stratifies anaesthesia EEG, acquired navigation, and post-anaesthesia sleep in sevoflurane-exposed mice
papers.abstract: Preoperative anxiety is common and has been associated with postoperative delirium, yet whether an anxious phenotype changes the brain's response to anaesthesia is unknown. Here, 42 mice are classified as low-anxiety (LA) or high-anxiety (HA) by fear-retrieval freezing and exposed to sevoflurane without surgery. When adequate anaesthetic effects are reached, HA mice show a higher aperiodic spectral edge frequency than LA mice. After anaesthesia, both groups retain choice accuracy in the Water Cross Maze, but in the same trials decomposed into behavioural syllables, the learned navigation sequence is selectively disrupted in HA mice. Rapid eye-movement sleep decreases in HA mice and increases in LA mice. A single anxiety phenotype defined before induction therefore tracks three responses to the same sevoflurane exposure. These findings suggest that pre-anaesthetic anxiety marks individual vulnerability to anaesthesia in mice. The results may pave the way to interventions preserving cognitive function and sleep during perioperative recovery.

papers.title: Compact SC-LIF: A factorized hybrid network for motor imagery EEG decoding.
papers.abstract: We develop a compact motor-imagery (MI) EEG decoder and examine its classification performance and computational cost. Compact SC-LIF combines factorized temporal-spatial convolutions with channel-adaptive spike-count leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. The primary BCI Competition IV 2a comparison evaluates six models using common input trials, identical training-session validation folds, equal search budgets, and three final seeds. Additional experiments examine BCI Competition IV 2b, Zhou2016, architectural components, and channel and neuron settings. Compact SC-LIF achieves 71.91 ± 12.93% subject-level accuracy and 71.72% macro-F1 with 3,508 parameters and 6.45 million dense synaptic MACs per trial. Accuracy differences from EEGNet and FBCNet are not significant; gains over corrected PLIF-SNN, Deep4Net, and ShallowFBCSPNet range from 8.24 to 10.10 percentage points (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0195). Separate fixed-protocol controls attribute a 29.0% reduction in counted operations to front-end factorization, while the matched backend comparison does not establish an independent SC-LIF accuracy gain. The decoder combines a small parameter count with competitive MI classification under a defined evaluation protocol. Its computational savings are architectural; dense synaptic counts exclude neuron-state and memory costs and do not represent measured hardware energy.

ai.reason: Emphasizes a very compact, CPU-friendly EEG decoder with efficient convolutions—lightweight efficient architecture broadly transferable to other EEG classification tasks.
ai.summary: Develops Compact SC-LIF, a factorized temporal-spatial convolutional spike-count LIF network for motor imagery EEG decoding, achieving 71.91% subject-level accuracy and 71.72% macro-F1 with 3,508 parameters and 6.45 million dense synaptic MACs per trial, with gains of 8.24-10.10 percentage points over several baselines and a 29.0% operation reduction attributed to front-end factorization.

papers.title: Sparse EEG neurodynamics of hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes with personal euglycemic baseline adaptation.
papers.abstract: Hypoglycemia alters cerebral electrophysiological activity, providing a physiological basis for EEG-based detection. However, translation toward subject-independent monitoring remains constrained by uncertain minimum input requirements, insufficiently characterized stability of sparse representations and their physiological associations, and inter-participant baseline variability. This study benchmarked 24 models spanning engineered-feature machine learning, feature-domain deep learning, and raw-waveform deep learning under leave-one-subject-out validation. Channel-Feature Sparsification was applied using a predefined performance-preservation criterion. Sparse representations were evaluated for selection stability, cross-paradigm concordance, and physiological association. Personal Euglycemic Baseline Adaptation (PEBA) was subsequently applied using a short personal euglycemic reference without participant-specific model retraining. LDA achieved the highest observed balanced accuracy within the engineered-feature paradigm, whereas Sinc-SSNET performed best in both deep-learning paradigms. Sparsification retained the F7 log-theta descriptor for LDA, the F7 channel row for feature-domain Sinc-SSNET, and two channels for raw-waveform Sinc-SSNET. F7 was retained across all three paradigms, and its log-theta descriptor increased during hypoglycemia in 30 of 34 participants (88.2%). PEBA improved balanced accuracy from 0.71 to 0.77 for LDA, from 0.68 to 0.83 for feature-domain Sinc-SSNET, and from 0.71 to 0.78 for raw-waveform Sinc-SSNET. Compared with the corresponding full-input models, reduced configurations decreased parameter counts by 88.51%-99.88%, parameter storage requirements by 87.20%-99.88%, and multiply-accumulate operations by 94.72%-99.91%. These findings demonstrate the preservation of hypoglycemia-related EEG information under a predefined sparsification criterion, while personal euglycemic normalization improves cross-participant discrimination. Physiological consistency and reduced computational requirements support further evaluation of compact EEG-based hypoglycemia detection. Independent cohorts, continuous glycemic-transition recordings, and native sparse EEG acquisition are required before prospective application.

papers.title: AI-Driven Non-Invasive Scalp EEG Biosensing for Real-Time Seizure Prediction Using Lightweight Gradient Boosting Ensembles.
papers.abstract: Clinical translation of non-invasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) seizure prediction is severely hindered by patient-dependency, elevated false alarm rates, and excessive computational latency. This study introduces a computationally lightweight, patient-independent machine learning pipeline designed to achieve cross-patient generalization and robust false alarm suppression without requiring subject-specific calibration. Using the continuous multi-channel scalp EEG dataset from the CHB-MIT benchmark (materials/setting), signals underwent dual-stage filtering (1-70 Hz bandpass, 60 Hz notch), artifact removal via Extended FastICA, and Common Average Referencing. Dimensionality was reduced via Principal Component Analysis (12 orthogonal components, >95.4% variance explained). Continuous streams were partitioned into 5 s sliding windows (90% overlap) to extract multi-domain temporal, spectral, and discrete wavelet features, subsequently pruned via ANOVA F-testing to 168 salient predictors. Pre-ictal transitions (20 to 5 min prior to seizure onset, incorporating an excluded 5 min prediction horizon buffer) were classified using a synchronized ensemble of regularized XGBoost and leaf-wise LightGBM models. Dual-model coincidence was governed by a 30 s moving temporal alignment window coupled with 12-epoch persistence smoothing and a 30 min refractory lockout. To prevent intra-subject data leakage, multi-session recordings from the same individual (Cases 01 and 21) were strictly co-located within the training set, and the pipeline was evaluated on an isolated cohort of four completely unseen subjects (Patients 20, 22-24) across 156.5 continuous, unsampled hours. On the independent unseen test cohort, the post-processed framework achieved a primary event-level seizure sensitivity of 100% (34/34 seizures detected; 95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 89.72-100.0%), mathematically bounded by the test sample size, with a false alarm rate of 0.415/h (an 89.5% reduction versus the raw ensemble) and a mean Seizure Prediction Horizon of 17.03 min. Under continuous 0.5 s sliding-window streaming (designed for real-time edge persistence filtering), the framework demonstrated 99.80% operational pre-ictal alert consistency (60,772/60,894 sliding windows; specificity: 98.64%, precision: 91.20%, F1-score: 95.31%). Evaluated on strictly independent, non-overlapping 5 s epochs (N = 6120), the ensemble retained a pre-ictal sensitivity of 99.1%, confirming robust performance independent of window overlap. Execution latency was 0.0057 ms per window, delivering a >1000× speedup over state-of-the-art 3D-CNN and Transformer architectures. By eliminating multi-session data leakage and mitigating clinical alarm fatigue, this pipeline offers reliable cross-patient generalizability, practical intervention timing, and ultra-low computational latency suitable for real-time deployment on low-power wearable closed-loop neurostimulation devices.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Objective. Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Approach. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method was evaluated under a written protocol, then re-designed as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, frozen with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, assessed by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, and applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database from Children's Hospital Boston; 101 evaluable seizures). Main results. The original method detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. The frozen scheme detected 15 of 45 development seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. In validation it detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Significance. Vigilance state, clock time and admission trend inflate apparent warning performance unless the chance model preserves that structure, and the short-horizon signal did not generalise beyond its development cohort. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

ai.topic: Seizure warning with locked evaluation and vigilance confounds
ai.reason: Demonstrates that vigilance state, clock time, and admission trends confound EEG prediction; useful cautionary methodology for state-aware evaluation, though focused on clinical seizure prediction rather than sleep staging.
ai.summary: Evaluated scalp EEG seizure warning in 21 monitored children under a pre-specified, locked protocol, finding the initial method (44% of seizures, 0.48 false alarms/hour) no better than chance. A redesigned state-conditioned scheme achieved 33% detection during cross-validation but failed to exceed structured chance in two external validation cohorts (19% detection at 0.60 false alarms/hour versus 26% chance), a negative result.

papers.title: DualBranchEEG: A Dual-Branch CNN BiLSTM Network with Temporal Attention and Spectral Features for Three Class EEG Seizure Classification
papers.abstract: Automated seizure detection from electroencephalography (EEG) is a key step toward closed-loop brain-computer interface (BCI) systems and clinical decision support. We present DualBranchEEG, a dual-branch network that fuses (i) a temporal branch--a three-block 1-D convolutional encoder, a two-layer bidirectional LSTM and an additive attention layer--operating on the raw z-scored waveform, with (ii) a spectral branch--an MLP on log-power spectral density (PSD) features from Welch's method. We evaluate three-class classification (normal, interictal, ictal) on the Bonn University EEG dataset (500 single-channel recordings, 173.61 Hz) using a single stratified 70/15/15 split (seed 42). We position this work as a transparent reference implementation and exploratory comparison, not as evidence of superiority. A CNN-BiLSTM baseline (728,387 parameters; last-time-step readout, no attention, no augmentation) attains 96.00% test accuracy (72/75) and a macro AUC-ROC of 0.9795; five-fold stratified cross-validation of this baseline gives 98.40 {+/-} 1.52% accuracy and 0.9952 {+/-} 0.0071 AUC-ROC. The full DualBranchEEG (823,556 parameters) attains the same 96.00% test accuracy, macro F1 of 0.9543 and macro AUC-ROC of 0.9952. In the ablation, CNN-only, BiLSTM-only and CNN+BiLSTM+attention variants each reach 94.67%, and the full model is one test recording better; with only 75 test recordings these differences lie within sampling uncertainty (95% Wilson interval for 96.00%: 88.9-98.6%). Band-power differences between all class pairs are significant in all five canonical EEG bands. Grad-CAM, t-SNE and attention visualisations are reported as qualitative diagnostics only. We document all known methodological limitations, including PSD standardisation fitted on all 500 recordings and Welch's default 50% segment overlap.

ai.reason: Combines spectral PSD features with a lightweight-ish deep model; transparent reference implementation is useful, though on a small Bonn dataset and seizure-focused.
ai.summary: Presents DualBranchEEG, a dual-branch CNN-BiLSTM with temporal attention fused with Welch log-power spectral features, for three-class seizure classification on the Bonn EEG dataset; the full model reached 96.00% test accuracy, macro F1 0.9543, and macro AUC-ROC 0.9952, comparable to a CNN-BiLSTM baseline that achieved 98.40% accuracy under five-fold cross-validation.

papers.title: Objective-to-Subjective Sleep Discrepancy in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Pilot EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep disturbance is common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the relationship between subjectively perceived and objectively measured sleep duration remains poorly understood. This pilot study aimed to compare objective and subjective total sleep time (TST) and to explore clinical factors associated with each measure and the difference between them. It also examined the relationship between this difference and nocturnal blood pressure regulation. Materials and Methods: Twenty-two hospitalized patients with RA underwent overnight sleep monitoring using a portable single-channel electroencephalography (EEG) device and provided subjective estimates of TST for the same night in response to a question asked the following morning. Sleep discrepancy was defined as subjective minus EEG-derived TST. Associations with clinical variables were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction. Exploratory regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index were performed. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was available for 20 patients. Results: Subjective TST exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min (p = 0.0008), and the two measurements were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.119, p = 0.598). A more positive signed sleep discrepancy was associated with lower serum albumin (ρ = -0.723, q = 0.0020), higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels (ρ = 0.624, q = 0.0134), glucocorticoid use (q = 0.0462), higher DAS28-CRP (q = 0.0495), and greater functional disability (q = 0.0495). Associations with albumin and CRP persisted in separate exploratory models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Patients with a conventional dipper blood pressure (BP) pattern had a lower signed sleep discrepancy than those with other nocturnal BP patterns (p = 0.0087). Conclusions: In this small exploratory study, subjective sleep duration in patients with RA was generally longer than EEG-derived sleep duration. Furthermore, preliminary associations were observed between sleep discrepancy and inflammatory and clinical characteristics, as well as with nocturnal BP patterns. These findings require confirmation in larger studies, and the clinical significance of sleep discrepancy remains uncertain.

papers.title: Cognitive load detection using hyper-learning dragonfly optimization for feature selection.
papers.abstract: Cognitive load detection is essential for understanding brain responses to mental effort and cognitive demands. Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals provide valuable information about neural activity and offer a non-invasive approach to identifying cognitive load. However, accurate detection and the identification of brain regions with superior discriminative capabilities remain important challenges. This study proposes an EEG-based cognitive load detection framework using empirical Fourier decomposition (EPFD), entropy-based feature extraction, and the hyper-learning binary dragonfly feature selection algorithm (HLBDA). EEG signals recorded from each brain lobe over four-second intervals were decomposed into 10 intrinsic mode functions (IMFs). Entropy-based features were extracted from the IMFs, and the most informative features were selected using HLBDA. The selected features were classified using machine learning (ML) classifiers. The proposed framework was evaluated on the MAT, STEW, and MLR datasets. Additionally, lobe-wise cognitive load detection was performed on the MAT and STEW datasets to investigate the discriminative capabilities of five individual brain lobes. Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) was employed to prevent data leakage. The proposed framework achieved classification accuracies of 97.13%, 96.48%, and 98.2% on the MAT, STEW, and MLR datasets, respectively, using the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) classifier for MAT and STEW and the ensemble subspace KNN (ESSK) classifier for MLR. In the lobe-wise analysis, the frontal lobe demonstrated superior discriminative capability for cognitive load detection, achieving accuracies of 96.7% and 96.6% on the MAT and STEW datasets, respectively, using the ESSK classifier. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed EPFD-HLBDA-based framework for EEG-based cognitive load detection across multiple datasets. The superior performance of the frontal lobe suggests its potential as a particularly informative region for distinguishing cognitive states. Furthermore, the use of subject-wise LOOCV strengthens the evaluation by reducing the risk of data leakage. Compared with recently reported methods, the proposed framework demonstrates competitive classification performance and highlights the potential of lobe-specific EEG analysis for reliable cognitive load assessment.

ai.reason: Empirical Fourier decomposition, entropy features, and optimization-based feature selection form a lightweight, transferable EEG classification pipeline.
ai.summary: Proposes an EEG-based cognitive load detection framework combining empirical Fourier decomposition, entropy-based feature extraction, and hyper-learning binary dragonfly feature selection (HLBDA), classified with KNN/ensemble subspace KNN. Achieved accuracies of 97.13%, 96.48%, and 98.2% on MAT, STEW, and MLR datasets, with the frontal lobe showing the strongest lobe-wise discriminative capability.

papers.title: Source-reconstructed EEG graph signal processing: Pitfalls and workarounds.
papers.abstract: Graph signal processing (GSP) enables studying brain structure-function coupling by examining how functional signals vary on the structural connectome (SC). While traditionally used with fMRI, GSP applied to electroencephalography (EEG) is gaining interest due to EEG's repertoire of brain activities and higher temporal resolution. To this aim, source activities are reconstructed through electrical source imaging (ESI), summarized into parcellated time series via singular value decomposition (SVD), and analyzed using graph Fourier transform based on SC Laplacian's eigenvectors. This study investigates two methodological biases: SVD polarity ambiguity and ESI spatial leakage. Using simulated epileptic spikes, we validated a method to resolve SVD sign ambiguity and tested it on real interictal epileptogenic discharges. We then quantified the leakage effect on simulation, by comparing graph power spectra between ground truth and its ESI reconstruction, across inverse solutions (exact low-resolution electrical tomography [eLORETA], vs. linear constraint minimal variance) conditions (baseline vs. spike), and connectomes (structural vs. Euclidean distance-based [EC]). We found that uncorrected polarity ambiguity increases high-frequency content, a bias mitigated by the proposed sign control. Conversely, ESI leakage inflates low-frequency content, with stronger effect during spikes, for eLORETA and EC. These results suggest caution in GSP-EEG analyses and inform analytical pipeline selection.

papers.title: Automated Interictal Epileptiform Discharge Detector Scores in Serial EEG: Record-Level Concordance Did Not Extend to Within-Participant Change.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAutomated deep learning-based interictal epileptiform discharge detectors have been validated for cross-sectional recognition, but longitudinal concordance is uncertain. We tested whether three distinct pretrained detectors agreed on direction and rank ordering of within-participant change in serial EEG.MethodsThis secondary analysis included 45 routine EEG recordings from 15 adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy at baseline, week 1, and month 3 in the active arm of a parent tDCS trial; treatment efficacy was not evaluated. SpikeNet1, SpikeNet2, and Cyclops used pretrained weights and detector-specific pipelines on identically staged 25-min intervals. The record-level endpoint was the unthresholded mean window score. Concordance was characterized using record-level and change-score Spearman correlations, directional agreement, and a standardized detector × time repeated-measures ANOVA.ResultsDescriptive record-level correlations ranged from ρ = 0.341 to 0.696. Change-score correlations ranged from -0.011 to 0.379 (week 1) and from -0.089 to 0.536 (month 3). All six were smaller in absolute magnitude than their record-level counterparts and nonsignificant after Holm adjustment. Three-detector directional agreement was 7/15 (week 1) and 6/15 (month 3). The detector × time interaction was nonsignificant (Greenhouse-Geisser-corrected p = .142). Post hoc tolerance zones did not increase three-detector agreement. Thresholded SpikeNet2 and Cyclops outputs were sparse, and high-threshold agreement reflected shared zero change.ConclusionsRecord-level concordance did not extend to within-participant change or establish longitudinal interchangeability of mean window scores. Even for validated detectors, a longitudinal finding from one detector should not be assumed to generalize across detectors without independent corroboration.Parent trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05951244), NCT05951244.

papers.title: Case Report: Clinical applications of extended-duration remote ambulatory EEG monitoring: lessons from real-world cases.
papers.abstract: Traditional ambulatory electroencephalography (EEG) and inpatient epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) admissions face significant operational limitations including: short recording windows (typically 24-72 h), high costs, technician shortages, and physical restrictions on daily activities. This article presents clinical utility frameworks and three illustrative real-world case studies utilizing the REMI Remote EEG Monitoring System-a wireless, wearable 4-sensor electrode-setup (10-channel EEG montage system) montage system integrated with cloud data transmission and post-acquisition artificial intelligence (AI) electrographic seizure detection algorithms. In Case 1, a 39-year-old female with suspected recurrent epilepsy experienced three focal seizures after the standard 72-h monitoring window, allowing initiation of targeted antiseizure therapy. In Case 2, extended monitoring in a 57-year-old male with long-standing epilepsy experiencing new exercise-induced symptoms ruled out electrographic seizures, avoiding unnecessary medication escalation. In Case 3, a 52-year-old male with worsening episodic déjà vu exhibited focal interictal rhythmic activity, providing objective data to guide shared decision-making and successful initiation of antiseizure treatment. Extended-duration remote EEG monitoring bridges key diagnostic gaps by offering flexible, real-world data collection over extended timeframes (up to 30 days). This approach optimizes clinical triage, clarifies event etiology, and improves ambulatory epilepsy care without overburdening tertiary health care infrastructure.

papers.title: Frequency-embedded sequence learning for multi-class EEG-to-text interface.
papers.abstract: A brain-computer interface (BCI) is an emerging technology for decoding users' intentions, enabling speech decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) signals. This study proposes a multi-class (i.e., 5 words or phrases) EEG-to-Text classification pipeline based on a lightweight 1-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) architecture. The model is trained using both time-domain EEG signals and frequency-embedded power spectral density (PSD) sequences, facilitating systematic comparison of feature representations. EEG signals were preprocessed using a bandpass filter (4 - 120 Hz) and a notch filter (60 Hz) followed by PSD estimation using the modified Welch method. The processed signals were then used to train the proposed 1D-CNN architecture designed for sequential data. In intra-subject evaluation, the proposed approach achieves classification accuracies (mean ± standard deviation) of 46.1 ± 5.1 and 64.4 ± 8.3 using time-domain EEG signals and frequency-embedded PSD sequences, respectively. Peak intra-subject accuracies reach 54% and 82% using EEG signals and PSD sequences, respectively. For inter-subject (pairwise) evaluation, the best observed accuracy is 42%. Inter-subject (pooled) performance remains near chance level (23.3 ± 1.0 and 24.5 ± 0.4), highlighting inter-subject generalization as a key challenge in EEG-based BCI systems. These results demonstrate that while intra-subject performance is promising, inter-subject generalization remains a major limitation. Overall, the proposed approach demonstrates the potential of frequency-embedded PSD representations for improving EEG-based imagined speech classification, while motivating further work toward robust, user-independent BCI systems.

papers.title: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition network based on moment channel attention.
papers.abstract: While most cross-subject EEG emotion recognition studies focus on average accuracy, the high inter-subject variability of EEG signals causes severe performance inconsistency across individuals. This inconsistency poses a critical barrier to real-world deployment but has received insufficient attention. To address this issue, this study proposes a hybrid emotion recognition model integrating moment channel attention and Transformer, termed the Moment Attention Convolution-Emotion Transformer Network (MAC-ETN). The proposed hybrid network consists of three components: a local temporal feature extractor, a Moment Channel Attention Network (MCA), and a global temporal feature extractor. Specifically, depthwise and separable convolutions are employed to extract local temporal features. The moment channel attention mechanism incorporates the first-order moment (mean), second-order moment (variance), and third-order moment (skewness) for channel importance calibration; and global dependency modeling is achieved through a Transformer encoder. Performance evaluation is conducted on two public datasets, DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI, using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV). The experimental results show that the main advantage of MAC-ETN lies in markedly reduced cross-subject performance variability rather than higher mean accuracy. On the DEAP dataset, the mean accuracy of MAC-ETN (61.26% for arousal and 60.47% for valence is lower than that of the strongest baselines reported under the same LOSO protocol, while its accuracy standard deviation (7.88% and 5.31%) is the lowest among all compared methods. On the MAHNOB-HCI dataset, the F1 standard deviation of MAC-ETN is 1.48% for arousal and 0.30% for valence, far below the values reported for the baselines in the literature, although the latter were obtained under a subject-dependent protocol and with a different F1 definition, so this comparison is indicative only. These results indicate that MAC-ETN reduces cross-subject performance variability at a moderate level of accuracy, which is relevant for practical EEG-based emotion recognition applications.

papers.title: Dynamic mesh pattern-based substance use addiction detection from EEG signals.
papers.abstract: An explainable EEG framework is presented to distinguish participants with substance use disorder (SUD) from healthy controls. Dynamic features are extracted. The signal relations retained by the model can also be traced. In Dynamic Mesh Pattern (DynMeshPat), a path is selected within a fixed local mesh according to the signal. Five vectors and four consecutive differences are converted into channel-rank sequences and transition features. In DynMeshPat-XFE, this representation is combined with cumulative weighted neighborhood component analysis (CWNCA). The t algorithm-based k-nearest neighbors classifier (tkNN) and Directed Lobish (DLob) are also used. The analysis was based on 1985 EEG segments: 904 SUD and 1081 control. These were obtained from 60 participants: 25 with SUD and 35 controls. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO CV) was used. All segments from each participant were assigned to one outer test fold. Feature selection was repeated within the LOSO procedure. The 22-column model achieved 99.45% segment-level accuracy. Balanced accuracy, macro F1-score, and geometric mean were 99.43%, 99.44%, and 99.43%, respectively. The Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) was 0.989. SUD sensitivity was 99.23%, and control specificity was 99.63%. A1, A2, and E were excluded before feature extraction. Segment-level accuracy then rose to 99.70%. The selected features were described with sensor-space symbols through DLob. The reported performance is segment-level and does not establish participant-level diagnostic accuracy or a validated cortical biomarker.

papers.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots.
papers.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4-8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

papers.title: Age-Adjusted Exploratory Analysis of Spectral, Aperiodic, and Microstate Electroencephalography Features in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can characterize functional brain alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS), but many EEG features vary with age. We, therefore, examined resting-state EEG associations with MS using age-adjusted models while explicitly accounting for the severe age imbalance in the available dataset. Resting-state 128-channel EEG data from the BrainLat dataset were analyzed. Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately to five global spectral/aperiodic tests, 16 global microstate tests, and the 128 channel-wise tests within each feature. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. After correction, diagnosis coefficients were significant for global bandwidth (β = 1.928, q = 0.0287), global aperiodic offset (β = 1.816, q = 3.29 × 10-7), and offset at all 128 channels (β range = 1.52-2.41; q range = 3.56 × 10-8 to 7.43 × 10-5). Global central frequency, exponent, power spectral density, and all 16 microstate measures did not survive FDR correction. No within-MS continuous-age or age-stratified result survived FDR correction. Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs. 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. The findings are exploratory and require age-matched replication with detailed clinical, vigilance, site, sex, and magnetic resonance imaging characterization.

papers.title: Predicting Seizure Recurrence After Withdrawal of Antiseizure Medications Through Electroencephalogram Connectivity Analysis: A Proof-of-Concept Study.
papers.abstract: BackgroundDetermining antiseizure medication (ASM) withdrawal in patients with prolonged seizure freedom is crucial, yet no reliable biomarker exists. Pediatric neurologists often rely on clinical risk factors and electroencephalogram (EEG) inspection to predict recurrence.MethodsWe applied EEG connectivity analysis using directed transfer function (DTF) to predict recurrence after ASM withdrawal in 63 patients (29 recurrence, 34 nonrecurrence). All patients were seizure-free for at least 2 years before their ASMs were withdrawn. Before ASM withdrawal, an EEG was obtained for each patient, and indicated the absence of epileptiform discharges. Classification was conducted with feature selection and five classifiers.ResultsThe statistical results revealed that the DTF connectivity in the motor regions, including the right primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4, BA4) and the left and right medial premotor regions (Brodmann area 6, BA6), was significantly higher in the recurrence group. The highest average performance across the five evaluated classifiers (sensitivity, 87.50%; specificity, 87.35%; accuracy, 87.28%; and AUC, 87.43%) was achieved when 16 DTF features were selected. Compared with the majority-class baseline of 53.97% (representing the proportion of the majority non-recurrence class, 34/63), all trained classifiers demonstrated vastly superior performance. Among these classifiers, SVM had the best individual performance index, achieving a sensitivity of 96.67%, specificity of 90.58%, accuracy of 93.36%, and AUC of 93.63% while 16 selected features were used.ConclusionsThe method effectively identified Brodmann areas with significant differences and built models distinguishing recurrence from nonrecurrence at the patient level.

papers.title: Physiology-Guided Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Motor-Imagery Recognition.
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery electroencephalography (EEG) decoding depends on rhythm-specific modulation, cue-locked temporal evolution, and structured electrode topology, yet many decoders treat EEG as a generic multichannel time series. (1) Background: A physiological prior that stays in preprocessing cannot constrain what the decoder represents, and spiking networks let such a prior act on the event code itself. (2) Methods: We introduce PG-SNN, which embeds EEG priors in the event code, spatial operator, temporal dynamics, and readout. A causal eventizer converts EEG into sparse, sign-preserving spikes using rhythm-sensitive, temporal-change, and montage-contrast operators; an electrode-prior graph restricts message passing to local montage adjacency and homologous inter-hemispheric coupling; and a multi-timescale adaptive spiking backbone represents rapid event transitions and slower mu/beta modulation. (3) Results: On BCI Competition IV-2a the model reaches 84.72% accuracy (kappa = 0.796), 2.56 and 5.64 percentage points above the strongest matched ANN and SNN baselines; on the EEGMMIDB four-class subject-independent protocol, it reaches 71.28% (kappa = 0.617), 3.86 points above the strongest matched ANN baseline, and a fifteen-variant ablation attributes the largest single effect to the event code. (4) Conclusions: Embedding sensorimotor physiology into event generation, spatial propagation, and spike dynamics is a practical route to compact motor-imagery decoders, within the limits of the two benchmarks and the single shared protocol.

papers.title: Multicentre electrophysiology reveals the limits of auditory prediction responses as biomarkers of chronic tinnitus
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers of chronic tinnitus remains challenging because ageing and hearing loss independently influence auditory cortical activity. Here, we investigated auditory expectation processing in 440 adults with (n = 226) and without (n = 214) chronic tinnitus using electroencephalography during a local-global auditory paradigm across six centres. Although several electrophysiological group differences emerged in unadjusted analyses, most were substantially attenuated after adjustment for demographic and audiological factors. Two clusters remained significant within the unexpected-omission-versus-sound contrast (44 to 100 ms and 356 to 476 ms), but neither survived correction across eight contrasts. Direct comparisons between expected and unexpected omissions revealed no significant group differences. Exploratory classification using selected EEG features achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.624, increasing to 0.689 when combined with demographic and audiological predictors. However, this improvement was not reproduced in held-out validation, and EEG features showed limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness. These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between electrophysiological group differences and clinically informative individual-level biomarkers, underscoring the importance of controlling for confounding factors and establishing independent predictive validity in tinnitus research.

Found that most electrophysiological group differences were attenuated after adjusting for demographic and audiological factors, and classification based on EEG features achieved cross-validated AUC of 0.624 (0.689 with demographic/audiological predictors) but limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness.

papers.title: Intraoperative Subcallosal Cingulate Local Field Potential Spectral Analysis During Emotion-Evoking Music in Treatment-Resistant Depression With Multitarget Deep Brain Stimulation: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: The subcallosal cingulate (SCC/sgACC) is a proposed target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and intraoperative local field potentials (LFPs) are being explored as a source of candidate biomarkers. We report a 52-year-old woman with early-onset, highly refractory TRD and comorbid obsessive-compulsive and anxiety disorders who underwent tractography-guided multitarget DBS with four 8-contact non-directional leads: two in the SCC and two along a trajectory through the posterior-ventral nucleus accumbens (NAc), the anterior bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), and the anterior limb of the internal capsule (ALIC). In this exploratory technical observation, LFPs were recorded from the macrocontact of a microelectrode in the left SCC of the awake patient, with stimulation OFF, during two music trials: one with a no-music baseline, two neutral songs (rock and classical), and her favorite (happy) song, and one with a baseline and a sad song. Spectra (Welch's method) and aperiodic exponents were compared post hoc, and broadband (3-45 Hz) power during each song was expressed relative to the baseline of the same trial. Verification of the raw data identified non-neural features that could mimic affective effects: the exported segments had been downsampled without anti-alias filtering, so 60-Hz mains interference appeared as narrow lines at 40 and 20 Hz, and 23 corrupted samples in the first 4 s of the happy-song segment inflated its power more than 200-fold. After their exclusion, broadband power relative to baseline was higher during the sad song (1.43-fold) than during the happy song (0.69-fold; between-song ratio 2.06, permutation p=0.024) and the rock song (0.57-fold; ratio 2.48, p=0.004), but not the classical piece (1.13-fold; p=0.45). Absolute power did not differ between the sad and happy songs, power rose transiently before the sad song began and remained elevated after it ended, and aperiodic exponents showed no valence-related pattern. Three months after stimulation onset, the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score decreased from 26 to 13 and the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale score from 19 to 8. This single-case observation provides, at most, a weak post hoc signal of valence-related SCC broadband activity and mainly shows how acquisition and export artifacts can mimic affective LFP effects. Raw-data verification, anti-alias filtering, and repeated, counterbalanced conditions are prerequisites for evaluating intraoperative SCC LFPs as candidate biomarkers.

papers.title: Brain rhythms during Instagram Reels viewing and subsequent performance on sustained attention and working memory: an EEG study
papers.abstract: What does even a short scrolling 'snack' do to the brain? Short-form video feeds such as Instagram Reels have been rapidly becoming a near-universal phenomenon, used widely by people around the world, especially young adults. However, this is a very recent development, and yet their immediate effects on brain activity, attention, and working memory remain unclear. In a counterbalanced, within-subject experiment, we examined whether 10 minutes of Instagram Reels altered electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, cognitive performance, and subjective fatigue. Thirty university students completed three testing blocks separated by two counterbalanced interventions selected from viewing Reels on their own accounts, viewing a silent sequence of neutral images on their phones, or resting with eyes closed. EEG was recorded using 65 electrodes during interventions and subsequent sustained-attention (SART) and working-memory (N-back) tasks. Compared with neutral images, Reels viewing was associated with higher posterior relative theta power and a lower posterior alpha-to-theta ratio. During the subsequent N-back, frontal relative alpha was higher after Reels than after neutral images. Fatigue increased more after Reels than after rest. One of four planned contrasts in the cleaned sample was significant. Brief Reels viewing was associated with differences in EEG activity compared with viewing neutral images, while no significant differences in attention or working-memory performance were detected after correction for multiple comparisons.

papers.title: Sensorimotor EEG Responses and Parietal Symmetry Objectively Reflect Ankle Kinesthesia and Position Sense in Healthy Middle-Aged and Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Objective assessment of ankle proprioception may clarify sensory contributions to post-stroke balance impairment. Position sense and kinesthesia are complementary, yet their stage-specific cortical correlates remain unclear. We combined joint position reproduction (JPR) and passive movement detection (PMD) within a passive dynamometer-electroencephalography (EEG) framework in 15 healthy middle-aged and older adults. After quality screening, 13 JPR and 14 PMD datasets were analyzed. Position sense was quantified by position matching error (ME), and kinesthesia by movement detection time (MDT). EEG quantified the brain symmetry index (BSI) during position encoding, event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) during reproduction, and movement-evoked N1 during movement detection. Lower parietal BSI was associated with smaller ME across the delta, theta, alpha, and broadband ranges (r = 0.603-0.854, p = 0.001-0.029). During position reproduction, mu/alpha- and beta-band power decreased over sensorimotor regions as the ankle approached the remembered target. Passive movement elicited a frontocentral N1 whose latency was positively associated with MDT at five midline electrodes (r = 0.570-0.803, p = 0.003-0.034). Position accuracy was linked to bilateral parietal organization and sensorimotor processing, whereas movement detection speed was linked to cortical response timing. These findings provide a physiological reference for ankle position sense and kinesthesia in healthy middle-aged and older adults based on averaged EEG features and their associations with behavioral performance, with single-trial reproducibility to be evaluated in future studies.

Lower parietal brain symmetry index was associated with smaller position matching error, and movement-evoked N1 latency was positively associated with movement detection time, providing physiological references for ankle proprioception.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of a Cap-Mounted Tripolar Concentric Ring Electrode System with a Central Gel-Delivery Opening for tEEG and EEG Recording.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) commonly uses conventional disc electrodes with conductive gel or paste to record electrical activity from the scalp. However, conventional disc electrodes have limited spatial selectivity because they detect electrical activity spreading from different brain regions. Tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCREs) have been developed to improve spatial selectivity by estimating the scalp surface Laplacian. Nevertheless, establishing electrical contact at hair-bearing scalp locations remains challenging. To address this challenge, we developed a modified gold-plated copper TCRE with a 2 mm central opening for conductive gel delivery and a custom 3D-printed cap-mounted holder. After electrode placement, conductive gel is delivered through the opening to establish electrical contact between the metallic contacts and the scalp beneath the hair. The system was evaluated in ten healthy adults using eyes-open/eyes-closed resting-state EEG and pattern-reversal checkerboard visual stimulation. For the experimental recordings, two modified TCREs were positioned at the occipital scalp locations O1 and O2, where conductive gel was delivered through their central openings to establish electrical contact with the scalp. A third TCRE was positioned at Pz and coupled using conductive paste, while a separate conventional disc electrode was placed 1 cm superior to Pz. Recordings from these electrode configurations were analyzed to evaluate resting-state alpha activity, visual evoked potentials (VEPs), and signal quality. Each TCRE provided tripolar EEG (tEEG) and EEG Emulator (eEEG) signals. The modified TCREs recorded identifiable VEP components, with negative and positive peaks near 105 and 141 ms, respectively, along with stimulus-related spectral activity. The eEEG VEP waveforms at O1 and O2 showed strong correlations with Pz eEEG (median r=0.897 and 0.938, respectively). Alpha-band power also increased significantly during eye closure in both gel-coupled tEEG channels (Holm-adjusted p=0.0195). Impedance measurements, signal-quality analyses, and circuit modeling provided additional characterization of the system. These findings support the feasibility of acquiring tEEG and eEEG signals using the modified TCRE system at hair-bearing scalp locations.

papers.title: Quantitative EEG Differences Across Two Sedation Conditions in a Child with Epilepsy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Sedation is frequently required to obtain electroencephalography (EEG) recordings in children with neurodevelopmental disorders and structural etiologies of epilepsy. However, the extent to which different sedative agents influence quantitative interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden remains insufficiently characterized. A child with congenital cytomegalovirus-associated structural brain injury underwent EEG recordings under two sedation conditions: continuous low-dose propofol infusion and oral chloral hydrate. Quantitative analyses were performed using a duration-matched, within-subject design. Artifact-minimized EEG segments of equal duration (15.52 min) were analyzed. IED burden was quantified using spike frequency (spikes/min) and spike index (percentage of 10 s epochs containing ≥1 spike). Spectral power distribution and spectral edge frequency (SEF95) were also evaluated. The chloral hydrate recording showed a higher observed spike frequency than the propofol recording (14.11 vs. 4.12 spikes/min; descriptive rate ratio, 3.42) and a higher 10-s spike index (84.95% vs. 27.96%). Spectral analysis demonstrated lower SEF95 and greater delta predominance in the propofol recording, whereas the chloral hydrate recording showed relatively greater theta-alpha activity. The two recordings showed marked differences in apparent IED burden and background spectral characteristics. However, because they were obtained approximately one year apart and under different clinical circumstances, including intercurrent illness during the chloral hydrate recording, these differences cannot be attributed specifically to the sedative agents. This case illustrates the importance of considering sedation, clinical context, and vigilance state when longitudinally interpreting quantitative pediatric EEG findings.

papers.title: Acute Effects of Prolonged Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation on Cortical Excitability: A Randomized Crossover TMS-EEG Study
papers.abstract: Background: prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation (piTBS), as used in Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), achieves antidepressant efficacy, yet its acute single-session mechanisms remain elusive. EEG can capture online oscillatory dynamics during piTBS and pre- to post-stimulation changes in TMS-evoked cortical reactivity. Methods: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial, 40 healthy males completed two visits ( [≥]7-day washout), receiving active or sham piTBS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Inter-train EEG power was analyzed across three blocks of 20 trains in 37 participants. Pre- and post-stimulation measures of TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), working memory and sustained attention were analyzed in all 40 participants. Results: left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks during active and sham piTBS (conditionxblock interaction, p = .014). During active piTBS, theta power was below baseline in blocks 1 and 2 and increased significantly from block 2 to block 3. Across conditions, alpha power was lower in blocks 2 and 3 than in block 1. Direct comparison of pre-to-post TEP changes between active and sham piTBS identified no significant clusters in the N45, P60, N100 and P180 component windows. Exploratory analyses within active piTBS identified a decrease in frontal N100 cluster amplitude and an increase in posterior N100 cluster amplitude. Neither behavioral outcome showed condition-dependent changes. Conclusion: a single session of active piTBS modulated left frontal theta power between stimulation trains. Whether this early response is associated with cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes following SNT warrants further investigation.

papers.title: Hybrid EEG-EOG Brain-Computer Interface for Virtual-Reality Powered Mobility Training in Children with Severe Neuromotor Disabilities: A Multiple-Case Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Developing Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) for children with severe neuromotor disabilities remains challenging due to developmental neurophysiology and the high cognitive demands of motor imagery. Hybrid BCIs integrating electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) can overcome these limitations by combining continuous motor-related control with reliable discrete commands. This multiple-case study investigated the feasibility of a hybrid EEG-EOG BCI integrated with a virtual reality (VR) powered wheelchair simulator for mobility training. Methods: Six participants (mean age: 13.00 ± 3.52 years; 1 female, 5 males) with severe neuromotor disabilities (i.e., Central Core Myopathy, LAMA2 related Congenital Muscular Dystrophy, Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type II, and Cerebral Palsy) completed repeated sessions using a self-paced BCI. The system combined continuous kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI) for steering and EOG-detected voluntary blinks for discrete commands. We evaluated online classification performance (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity), user workload (NASA-TLX), and simulator-related discomfort (MSAQ) under fully and semi-immersive VR conditions. Results: Across the selected session-level evaluations, mean online classification accuracy was 67%, increasing to 77% when considering only successful evaluations. Four of the six participants completed the experimental protocol, whereas two discontinued after T3 because sufficiently stable BCI control could not be achieved. NASA-TLX scores indicated increasing perceived workload but generally low frustration, while low MSAQ scores suggested good VR tolerability. No participants withdrew because of VR-related discomfort or adverse effects. Conclusions: This exploratory study provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility of hybrid EEG-EOG BCI control within a VR-based powered mobility simulator for children and adolescents with severe neuromotor disabilities. Although simulated navigation was feasible for four participants, substantial variability in BCI control highlights the need for further technological refinement and validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: From hemodynamics to function: the role of fNIRS and hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems in next-generation assistive technologies for rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Assistive technologies (AT) serve as fundamental tools for rehabilitation because they help people with neurological or physical disabilities to restore their abilities, independence and their overall life satisfaction. Existing AT control methods, which include manual operation, eye tracking, voice commands, electromyography (EMG) and electroencephalography (EEG), have improved rehabilitation results but still face challenges because of their inability to maintain reliable performance during user exhaustion and difficulties operating in challenging situations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has recently become a new neuroimaging technique that provides excellent imaging capability, can be used while moving, and has portable design features. fNIRS-based devices such as wheelchairs, robotic prostheses, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have proven their ability to decode user intention and assist rehabilitation. The limited ability of fNIRS to measure time intervals prevents its use in real-time systems. The hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems combine EEG technology, which provides high-speed temporal measurements, with fNIRS technology, which provides spatial and hemodynamic measurements. The multimodal techniques combine different measurement methods, which improve accuracy while decreasing false positive results and increasing system adaptability. This review critically examines how AT control modalities have been evolving, and it also measures what fNIRS can do technically, plus what it struggles with, and then it pulls together the available evidence on hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems as a possible way toward more adaptive, user-centered rehabilitation technologies.

papers.title: Differential Neurophysiological Signatures of Asymptomatic Carotid and Intracranial Atherosclerotic Stenosis: A Multimodal Resting-State EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion associated with asymptomatic atherosclerotic cerebrovascular stenosis may induce functional-network alterations before overt neurological deficits emerge. Asymptomatic carotid stenosis (ACS) and asymptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (aICAS) represent distinct large-artery phenotypes with differing perfusion distributions. However, whether these location-specific hemodynamic constraints are associated with different patterns of functional brain reorganization is poorly understood. This study investigated the multiscale electrophysiological alterations associated with ACS and aICAS. In this cross-sectional study, 68 participants, including ACS (n = 29), aICAS (n = 17), and age-matched healthy controls (n = 22), underwent resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) recording and neuropsychological assessment (Chinese Mini-Mental Status [CMMS], Trail Making Test Parts A and B [TMT-A/B]). Microstate dynamics, power spectra, and α-band source-space functional connectivity were analyzed. Network-Based Statistic (NBS) controlled for family-wise error in connectivity analysis. Partial correlations adjusted for age, hypertension, and diabetes. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance was evaluated using bootstrap confidence intervals and repeated five-fold cross-validation. CMMS scores did not differ among groups, whereas TMT completion times were longer in the ACS group, indicating subtle performance alterations. Both patient groups showed reduced microstate A (MsA) coverage and decreased transitions between MsA and microstate C (MsC). ACS additionally exhibited shortened MsA duration, reduced α-band power, and increased connectivity within a distributed network identified by NBS. The aICAS group showed increased bidirectional transitions between microstate B (MsB) and microstate D (MsD) but no significant NBS component. Selected microstate measures remained associated with TMT performance after covariate adjustment. ROC analyses showed moderate discrimination, with apparent areas under the curves (AUCs) of 0.672-0.744 and cross-validated AUCs of 0.675-0.744. ACS and aICAS showed shared and location-specific electrophysiological alterations. These exploratory findings may help characterize early functional brain changes associated with asymptomatic cerebrovascular stenosis, but require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

Selected microstate measures remained associated with Trail Making Test performance and yielded moderate cross-validated ROC discrimination (AUC 0.675–0.744).

papers.title: A case of dissociative disorder with attenuation of EEG alpha power during a depersonalization episode.
papers.abstract: Dissociative disorders are characterized by disruptions in consciousness, memory, identity, and perception. Similar symptoms can occur in patients with frontal lobe epilepsy. Although dissociative disorders are generally classified as psychiatric conditions, several studies have reported electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities in only a small proportion of affected patients. The relationship between EEG abnormalities and dissociative symptoms remains poorly understood; further accumulation of similar cases is therefore required. We present the case of an adolescent female with a dissociative disorder, who had experienced depersonalization symptoms since childhood and developed recurrent episodes following COVID-19. The available clinical, magnetic resonance imaging, and scalp video-EEG findings did not support a diagnosis of epilepsy. Inpatient 24-h video-EEG monitoring at age 15 revealed a widespread reduction in alpha power across the brain during an episode of depersonalization. Previous studies have implicated alpha power in the maintenance of stable perceptual states. In this case, quantitative EEG analysis captured a transient widespread reduction in alpha power coinciding with the patient's depersonalization symptoms. Although the specificity, causality, and reproducibility of this finding remain unknown, it may reflect the patient's dissociative symptoms. This case report suggests that a patient's subjective experiences can be captured using objective neurophysiological measures such as EEG.

papers.title: EEG morphology and peri-ictal MRI abnormalities in status epilepticus and ictal-interictal continuum.
papers.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency that may have long-term consequences. Peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (PMAs) may serve as marker of potential acute ictal brain injury and can be used for estimating the risk of SE-defining electroencephalography (EEG) patterns. We hypothesized that excitatory-predominant EEG morphologies reflect higher metabolic demand and a greater likelihood of PMAs than inhibitory-predominant morphologies. In this single-center prospective cohort (February 2019-April 2025), we included patients who had either SE or ictal-interictal continuum (IIC) reported on EEG and underwent acute magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (≤48 h). Excitatory-predominant morphology was defined by a sharp-wave amplitude greater than those of the positive and slow wave, a broad sharp wave (>200 ms), or superimposed fast activity. Inhibitory-predominant morphology was defined by the positive or slow-wave amplitude greater than that of a sharp wave. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between EEG morphology and PMAs on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho assessed correlations between the number of excitatory features (0-2) and MRI sequences showing PMAs (none, arterial spin labeling [ASL] hyperperfusion only, or DWI/FLAIR). Among 205 included patients (134 IIC, 71 SE), excitatory-predominant patterns and lateralized periodic discharges were associated with increased risk of DWI/FLAIR PMAs (p = .001 and p = .02, respectively). In IIC patients, excitatory-predominant morphology was the only predictor of PMAs (p = .002). In the subset with ASL, DWI, and FLAIR sequences (n = 145), the number of excitatory features correlated strongly with types of sequences affected by PMAs (Kendall's tau p < .001; Spearman's rho p < .001). Excitatory-predominant morphology, as opposed to inhibitory-predominant patterns, was associated with a more frequent occurrence of PMAs. These findings support an EEG morphology framework based on excitatory-inhibitory balance across IIC and SE.

papers.title: Cognition in 6-17-year-olds with Generalized and Focal Pharmaco-responsive Non-structural Epilepsies and its Correlates on Diffusion Tensor Imaging and Quantitative EEG: A Comparative Observational Study.
papers.abstract: The study compares cognition and its correlates on diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and quantitative electroencephalogram (qEEG) between generalized and focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies and evaluates behavioral comorbidities. The study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in north India in 20 generalized and 30 focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies in 6- to 17-year-olds. Cognition was tested using Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-IV (WISC-IV) and Stroop test and behavior was evaluated using Childhood Behavior Checklist (CBCL). All the cases underwent DTI and a subset underwent resting and task-based qEEG evaluation. Cognition scores were comparable between generalized and focal epilepsies; however, both showed significant impairment compared with historical controls. On DTI, fractional anisotropy of corpus callosum (body in focal and splenium in generalized) and cingulate cortex (in both) correlated significantly with cognition scores. On resting qEEG, cognition scores correlated negatively with absolute α, δ (focal epilepsy), β and θ powers (generalized epilepsy), and positively with α and δ powers (generalized epilepsy). Performance on task-based qEEG showed negative correlation with absolute delta power in both. Impaired CBCL scores were seen in 25% generalized and 16.7% focal epilepsies. Similar correlates on DTI and qEEG for generalized and focal epilepsies highlight the effect of network model of epilepsy on cognition. The negative correlation of α and β powers with WISC-IV and Stroop scores probably indicates an underlying anxious, tensed, and inattentive state leading to impaired performance in these tests. These cases should be routinely screened for behavioral comorbidities providing a therapeutic target for cognition.
