papers.title: Changes in Clinical Management Related to Continuous Versus Routine Electroencephalogram in Critically Ill Adults: Analysis of a Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) is increasingly utilized in the intensive care unit for consciousness-impaired patients with various conditions. It is, however, costly in terms of technical and human resources, and its impact on prognosis compared with routine EEG (rEEG) remains debated. We aimed to characterize the effect of cEEG vs. rEEG on clinical management modifications, and to determine if these correlated with a better outcome. This is an ancillary analysis using data of CERTA (NCT03129438), a randomized trial comparing cEEG versus repeated rEEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness. Clinical management modifications due to the EEG intervention, predefined as performed within 60 h of EEG start, were prospectively recorded (anti-seizure medication [ASM], sedation, new radiological examination, new surgical intervention, withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy). Correlation with the EEG type was analyzed by 2 × 2 tables; Mantel-Haenszel tests explored the impact on mortality and functional outcome at 6 months. The trial included 364 patients completing follow-up (182 each in the cEEG and rEEG groups). While 58.2% of cEEG and 45.6% of rEEG patients had any management change (p = 0.018), ASM was modified in 22.0% (cEEG) and 12.1% (rEEG) (p = 0.012); other clinical interventions were comparable across EEG groups. Adjusting for ASM modifications, mortality (p = 0.845) and functional outcome (p = 0.619) remained similar between the EEG groups. In critically ill adults, cEEG is associated with more clinical management modifications compared to repeated rEEG, particularly regarding ASM, but this does not seem to translate into improved patients' outcomes.

papers.title: The utility of additional electrodes during stereo-electroencephalography for pediatric epilepsy surgery.
papers.abstract: There is increasing use of stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) for invasive seizure onset zone (SOZ) localization in children due to its broad, three-dimensional, network-based sampling and improved tolerability compared with other strategies of invasive electrodes. However, initial SEEG does not always result in definitive SOZ localization, and diagnostic yield varies depending on patient selection and institution-specific factors. This study explores the benefits of additional electrodes to define the SOZ during the same hospitalization when initial SEEG sampling is insufficient for surgical planning in children. A cohort of patients who underwent additional electrode placement during the same hospitalization was identified from a database of pediatric epilepsy surgery cases performed between 2015 and 2025. Charts were retrospectively reviewed to obtain variables of interest, including demographics, electrode placement, and surgical outcomes. Fourteen patients underwent additional electrode placement during the same hospitalization. Reasons for additional electrodes include refining surgical resection margins (50%), inconclusive lobar localization (42%), and inconclusive lateralization (7%). Patients had an average of 11 initial and 3 additional electrode arrays implanted. Patients were monitored for seizure activity on average for 7 days for initial electrodes and an additional 4 days following additional electrode implantation. Following SEEG evaluation, patients underwent either laser ablation (50%), surgical resection (42%), or both (8%). Two patients did not proceed to surgery. Of the 12 patients who underwent surgery, 9 patients (75%) had a most recent follow-up outcome of ILAE 1-3. Additional electrode placement during the same hospitalization in this pediatric SEEG cohort was well tolerated with few observed minor complications and is particularly useful when electrodes are added to define surgical margins. Insights from additional electrodes influence subsequent surgical strategy, allowing more limited resections or laser ablations. These findings may contribute to attaining best practices for additional electrode use in pediatric SEEG patients. Stereotactic electrode placement is being increasingly used to define seizure origin in children with medication-resistant epilepsy, but it can fail to localize seizures in some cases. Placement of additional electrodes during the same hospitalization was associated with few observed minor complications in children and can help refine the surgical plan, allowing for more targeted surgery and may prevent the need for a second epilepsy surgery.
